subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Gulf Stream and Europe's Warmth
description: Learn The Gulf Stream and Europe's Warmth in one minute.

hook.text: London sits at the same latitude as Labrador, Canada. London is mild. Labrador is frozen.

buildup.text: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico northeast toward Europe.

discovery.text: This warm current raises northwestern Europe's temperature by 5 to 10°C above what it should be.

twist.text: Melting Greenland ice is adding fresh water to the North Atlantic, weakening the Gulf Stream.

climax.text: The current has already slowed by about 15% since the mid-20th century.

punchline.text: Europe's mild winters depend on a current that's losing its strength.

quiz.question: Why is Europe warmer than regions at the same latitude?
options: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the tropics
The ozone layer is thicker over Europe

details.summary: The Gulf Stream is a powerful Atlantic current that carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico toward northwestern Europe. This heat transfer keeps European winters significantly milder than those at the same latitude in North America.
details.whyItMatters: Europe's mild climate, agriculture, and ecosystems depend on the Gulf Stream. Any weakening could drastically cool the region even as the rest of the planet warms.
takeaways: The Gulf Stream carries warm tropical water northeastward
It makes Europe up to 10 degrees C warmer than its latitude suggests
Fresh meltwater from Greenland threatens to slow the current

faq.question: How warm does the Gulf Stream keep Europe?
faq.answer: Without the Gulf Stream, cities like London and Oslo could experience winters similar to Labrador in Canada, which sits at the same latitude. The current delivers roughly a petawatt of thermal energy to the North Atlantic region.

faq.question: Is the Gulf Stream slowing down?
faq.answer: Observations suggest the broader Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which includes the Gulf Stream, has weakened by about 15 percent since the mid-twentieth century. Greenland's accelerating ice loss is a key contributor.
